correctness.rationale: At fixed n>=2 and total S with all incomes positive integers, ordering by Gini is exactly ordering by integer D=sum_{i<j}|x_i-x_j|, and ordering by population CV squared is exactly ordering by Q=sum_i (n x_i-S)^2. Since positive profiles are all partitions of S into n parts and n<=S, exhaustive independent enumeration of all nondecreasing partitions and every same-(n,S) unordered pair for 2<=S<=12 is a complete finite proof. Exactly 762 pairs occur, zero strict oppositely ranked pairs through S=11, and exactly one at S=12: A=(1,2,4,5), B=(2,2,2,6), with D(A)=14>D(B)=12 and Q(A)=160<Q(B)=192. The first weak-order difference at S=10 is (1,4,5) vs (2,2,6), a Gini tie but differing CV. Two-household V=2G holds identically.

evidence: Classic treatments establish formulas and transfer sensitivities and comparisons of rankings under empirical populations.
No accessible primary claim asserts the complete positive-grid cutoff for all same-(n,S) pairs.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Broad inequality-theory results explain why measures can disagree, but generic non-equivalence does not imply sharp S=12 or uniqueness.

originality.rationale: Sen, Allison and Bendel et al. establish standard measure definitions and different rank/tail sensitivities, not the smallest strictly positive integer total at fixed household count and total, or the uniquely first reversal and tie splitting. A related Gini–variance inequality covers a different invariant, not this integer-grid order comparison. The result compares ordinal scores and does not identify welfare preference.

value.rationale: The first discrete-resolution limit at which two widely used and Lorenz-consistent yet distinct inequality statistics strictly disagree is a naturally motivated complete finite boundary. The small number 12 is not selected arbitrarily: exhaustive classification proves minimality and a unique witness, useful as a sharp reproducible cautionary example in inequality measurement.

limitations: Full-text Bendel 1989 and Sen chapter were not thoroughly inspected; an example or exercise with identical integer cutoff might be missed.
The sharp 12-unit boundary assumes fixed n, fixed S and positive integer incomes; allowing zero entries or arbitrary reals changes minimum.
The result compares ordinal scores and does not identify welfare preference.
